assumptions: all graphs with <= 7 vertices (networkx atlas) as candidate factors; composites of order n <= 15 are exactly the products of primes of orders whose product is n (n in 4,6,8,9,10,12,14,15)
graph counts A000088 / A001349 taken from the OEIS (cached) to turn composite counts into prime counts
falsification: A connected (resp. co-connected) graph with two different factorisations into connected (resp. co-connected) primes for one of the six commutative unital products.
hypothesis: H-C14-3 (bold, Inventor): each of the six commutative unital associative products has unique prime factorisation on connected graphs (Cartesian: Sabidussi-Vizing; strong: Doerfler-Imrich/McKenzie) or, for the complement-duals, on co-connected graphs. H-C14-7: Cartesian-prime and strong-prime connected graphs are equinumerous in every order (forced by unique factorisation and the common count of connected graphs).
methodology: For each product: find the composite graphs of orders 4 and 6 among the atlas graphs, take the rest as primes, enumerate all prime factorisations (multisets for commutative products, sequences otherwise) of every order <= 15, classify the products up to isomorphism, and record classes with more than one factorisation; repeat inside the class of connected graphs; verify the classical 63-vertex Cartesian counterexample (K1+K2+Q2)(K1+Q3) = (K1+Q2+Q4)(K1+K2).
question: For each associative local product with two-sided unit K1, which graphs of order <= 15 are composite, how many primes are there of each order, and where does unique factorisation fail?
